source: Wang & Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length
finding: Streams of key-value updates on the same key; only the last value is asked. Accuracy falls log-linearly toward zero as stale updates pile up, in every model tested.
numbers: Updates per key 3 to 400, 46 keys fixed. Large models start near 100%. At 400 updates the M tier falls to about 0% while the L tier stays relatively high. Over 30 LLMs.
quote: retrieval accuracy declines log-linearly toward zero as interference accumulates
limits: Synthetic key-value task. The target sits right before the query, so search difficulty is low. Absolute accuracy shifts with prompt wording; the trend does not.
agent_relevance: Many stale, similar entries under one cue can sink recall of the current one even when it is nearest the query. Cap entries per cue.

source: Wang & Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length
finding: Interference, not input length, drives the loss. With total input length held constant, more interfering updates still lowers accuracy. Experiment 3 shows one interference capacity limit with step-like collapse.
numbers: Regression on Interference Endurance Score (N=30 models): parameter size class t=3.03, p=0.005; context length t=-0.144, p=0.886; R2=0.261. Models with 128k-131k context only (N=19): Spearman rho=0.673, p=0.0016.
limits: Reasoning models were excluded from the regression. Chattaraj & Raj (b06) find a much weaker size effect with 39 models incl. more MoE.
agent_relevance: A longer context window does not buy resistance to stale-entry interference. Pruning matters more than window size.

source: Wang & Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length
finding: Telling the model to forget did not work. A per-key 'forget all previous updates' prompt, a forward-focus prompt, a relevance meta-prompt and a soft session reset gave marginal gains. The per-key forget prompt anchored errors at the instruction point and hurt gpt-4.1-mini.
numbers: Only a 'mock QA reset' (fake user turn asking for all keys, fake assistant reply, new task start) raised accuracy substantially, and accuracy still declined with update count. 46 keys, key-value length 6.
quote: LLMs exhibited no meaningful capacity for selective modulation of their retrieval processes under interference
limits: A mock turn boundary cuts the influence of all prior content; the authors say this is unusable when tasks need selective access to history. Directed forgetting works in humans, not here.
agent_relevance: An instruction like 'ignore old lessons' is weak. Remove stale entries from the context, or insert a hard task boundary.

source: Wang & Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length
finding: Errors are structured, not random. At low interference the wrong answers are earlier values of the same key. At high interference errors spread to off-target values (hallucinations), and a large share stays anchored to the earliest values.
numbers: Response distributions plotted for gemini-2.0-flash and gpt-4.1-mini at 12 and 281 updates; in the forget-prompt test only the instructed keys show error clusters at the forget position (20 updates per key, 46 keys; 19 position bins).
limits: Binned plots, no test statistic for this point.
agent_relevance: Stale items win because they are similar and stored, not because they are random noise. This matches the human cue-overload view.

source: Chattaraj & Raj (2026) LLMs Remember First, Forget Last: Dual-Process Interference in Large Language Models
finding: Across 39 LLMs, proactive interference (recall the latest value) is far worse than retroactive interference (recall the first value after updates). This is the reverse of the usual human finding, where new material overwrites old more than old blocks new.
numbers: PI vs RI Cohen's d=1.73, p<0.0001. RI accuracy 93.9% at N=3, 96.0% at N=50, 72.9% at N=100, 45.5% at N=200, 24.6% at N=300. PI falls from 94% to 3%. Mean offset +69.5 points.
quote: PI causes substantially greater degradation than RI
limits: Synthetic key-value paradigm, not human paired associates. N is update count, not list count. Authors name it a primacy bias in attention.
agent_relevance: For an LLM agent, old lessons block new ones (PI) more than new ones erase old (RI). Placing the newest entry near the query does not rescue it.

source: Chattaraj & Raj (2026) LLMs Remember First, Forget Last: Dual-Process Interference in Large Language Models
finding: Scale predicts RI resistance but not PI resistance. Context window length predicts neither. The two scores are almost independent, which suggests separate mechanisms.
numbers: Parameters vs RI R2=0.491 (beta=0.70, p<0.0001); largest tier (>500B) 171.2 vs smallest (<10B) 142.8, F(3,35)=11.83. Parameters vs PI R2=0.06, p=0.14. Context length vs RI R2=0.003. RI-PI correlation r=0.21, 95% CI [-0.11, 0.49], p=0.20.
limits: Contradicts the size effect on PI (R2=0.26) in b02. Authors blame more MoE models, whose total parameter count overstates capacity.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a bigger base model to remove the interference problem. Design the memory scaffold for it.

source: Chattaraj & Raj (2026) LLMs Remember First, Forget Last: Dual-Process Interference in Large Language Models
finding: Error profiles differ. RI errors are passive retrieval failures; PI errors are active intrusions of the earliest value (primacy). Hallucination is rare. PI collapses bimodally at high load (each session near ceiling or near floor); RI decays smoothly.
numbers: RI errors: retrieval failure 50.8%. PI errors: intrusion 56.1%. Hallucination 0.9% of RI errors and 0.2% of PI errors. 8.6% of PI failures contain explicit refusals vs 0% for RI. PI at N>=200 alternates between >85% and <5%. Best-fit curve: exponential 35% of models, polynomial 30%, log-quadratic 26%, power-law 9%.
limits: The winner-take-all attention mechanism is an interpretation, not tested by intervention.
agent_relevance: Failures look like confident use of an old item. A guard 'is there a newer entry for this cue?' is a targeted check.

source: Chattaraj & Raj (2026) LLMs Remember First, Forget Last: Dual-Process Interference in Large Language Models
finding: Reasoning models help with RI but not clearly with PI. Model families differ a lot in the PI/RI balance.
numbers: Six reasoning models (o1, o1-preview, o3, o3-mini, o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1) RI score 178.0 (SD 12.6) vs 150.3 (SD 18.2) for 33 standard models, +18.4%, t(37)=3.54, p=0.001, d=1.76. o1: RI 186.4 vs PI 22.0 (8.5x gap). GPT-5: 1.9x gap. Claude-4.5-opus: RI 178.4, PI 170.3 (1.05x gap).
limits: One scoring scheme and adaptive bootstrap sessions; model names as reported by the authors.
agent_relevance: Some designs are nearly immune to PI on this task. Measure our own model on this probe before choosing library caps.

source: Shahrabi-Farahani & Rahmati (2026) Compress and Forget: bitsandbytes Quantization Amplifies Proactive Interference in LLMs
finding: Extension of PI-LLM. 4-bit quantization lowers accuracy under high interference in all three open 7B-class models, only for semantically similar distractors. A numeric-distractor control shows no loss, with the sign reversed.
numbers: INT4 vs FP16, Qwen2.5-7B: 81.0% to 68.3%. Paired McNemar p<=2.6e-6. Same-key intrusion errors 21.5% to 24.6% of trials (p=4.8e-7). INT8 had a smaller penalty in 2 of 3 models. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Phi-3.5-mini; k=1 to 96 overwrites.
limits: Small models, one quantizer. Ablation places the effect in the quantized backbone, not the output layer. Not tested on frontier models.
agent_relevance: On a small or compressed model the interference limit is tighter. Semantic similarity is the driver, which supports varying category.

source: Wang & Sun (2025) versus Chattaraj & Raj (2026): disagreement on size
finding: Rival findings on what predicts PI resistance. Wang & Sun find parameter size predicts it; Chattaraj & Raj, with 39 models and more MoE, find it does not.
limits: Different model sets, task details and scoring. No head-to-head on the same models.
agent_relevance: Treat 'bigger is safer' as unproven for PI.

source: Xie (2026) Learning to Forget: Sleep-Inspired Memory Consolidation for Resolving Proactive Interference in LLMs (SleepGate)
finding: Proposes a learned forgetting gate and consolidation over the KV cache, with a conflict-aware tagger for superseded entries. In a tiny proof of concept it solves PI where five baselines fail.
numbers: 4-layer, 793K-parameter transformer on synthetic PI sequences. SleepGate 99.5% at PI depth 5, 97.0% at depth 10; full KV cache, sliding window, H2O, StreamingLLM and decay-only all below 18% at all depths. Claims interference horizon O(n) to O(log n) under mild assumptions.
limits: Preliminary, synthetic, toy scale, single author. No test on real LLMs or natural text; theory not tested at scale.
agent_relevance: The idea to copy: tag when a new entry supersedes an old one, then evict the old one.

source: Li et al. (2025) Sculptor: Empowering LLMs with Cognitive Agency via Active Context Management
finding: Giving the model tools to fragment, fold (summarize and hide) and search its own context raises accuracy on PI-LLM and NeedleBench without training. RL training raises it further.
numbers: PI-LLM average for Claude-4-Sonnet 84.04 to 89.94 (+5.90) with the tools (table text is garbled in extraction; row mapping uncertain). Sculptor-M3 vs base M3: +49.3 points on PI-LLM; after GSPO training 99.4% on PI-LLM. MemAgent 41.5% on PI-LLM.
limits: Gains vary by model and need benchmark-specific tool prompts. With a generic prompt Claude-4-Sonnet used search_context for 90.7% of tool calls; with a PI-specific prompt fold_fragment calls rose to 1206 and search fell to 625.
agent_relevance: Active hiding of obsolete entries works better than telling the model to ignore them (compare b03). Evidence for a 'fold stale lesson' operator.

source: Ding et al. (2026) Controlled Memory Interference in Continual LLM Agents
finding: Quantity of memory alone has limited effect. Relationship-specific interference (repeated history, same-slot conflict) sharply cuts the agent's ability to adopt updates (plasticity). Dense and lexical retrieval fail in different ways.
numbers: TravelPlanner noise-only growth: plasticity 0.510 (L0) to 0.455 (L6), stability 0.200 to 0.290, non-monotonic. At count 8 vs baseline P0=0.84, S0=0.92: Lexical repeated history plasticity -0.34, same-slot conflict -0.50; Dense unrelated -0.18, repeated history -0.46, same-slot conflict -0.44; Dense same-slot conflict stability 0.92 to 0.54 (-0.38).
limits: DeepSeek-v4-pro, temperature 0, reasoning off; these tables come mainly from one benchmark. Authors do not claim human and AI mechanisms match.
agent_relevance: Near-duplicate or conflicting entries hurt more than unrelated ones. Supports capping similar entries per class; dense retrieval is more exposed to semantic crowding.

source: Ding et al. (2026) Controlled Memory Interference in Continual LLM Agents (poisoning and training use)
finding: Memory poisoning depends more on update-authority cues than on recency. Training a selector on interference-labelled cases improves telling valid updates from interfering ones.
numbers: No decrease in matched-unnoised point estimates when CMI data is added. Evaluation on PERMA, HorizonBench, MEME Tracking (50 scenarios each) plus 1,000 fixed-L3 poisoning instances.
limits: Point estimates on small scenario counts; intervals are wide in places.
agent_relevance: Record what authorised a lesson and whether it supersedes another, not only when it was stored.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: An Empirical Study of Experience-Following Behavior
finding: Agents copy the output of the most similar stored experience (experience-following). Adding every run to memory (add-all) lets wrong runs propagate, and the gap to an error-free memory widens over time. Storage quality and size interact.
numbers: Compared add-all, coarse evaluators (three GPT variants) and strict selective addition; deletion by periodic, history-based and combined rules. A search summary reports about +10% average absolute gain for selective add plus delete over naive growth (not re-checked in the table). AgentDriver with strict selective addition passes the error-free variant after about 2000 executions.
limits: RegAgent and AgentDriver style settings; copying is driven by high input similarity. Per-task numbers were not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Near-duplicates trigger copying, including copying mistakes. Gate admission by quality and delete low-utility entries.

source: Arjmandi (2026) Distractor-Aware Truncation: Disentangling Context-Length Effects from Signal Loss in Long-Context LLM Benchmarks
finding: Removing distractors while keeping the answer evidence preserves or improves accuracy; naive middle-dropping collapses it because it deletes the signal. Shorter context helps only when what is cut is distractor.
numbers: BABILong, full to 25% retention (naive): Haiku -0.138, Sonnet -0.175, Opus -0.433, GPT-5.5 -0.613; GraphWalks -0.352/-0.427/-0.407/-0.397 (Holm padj<0.05 in 8 cells). Distractor-aware: Haiku +0.083 (padj=0.003), Sonnet +0.104 (padj<0.001), Opus +0.008, GPT-5.5 +0.017 (both at ceiling). bAbI facts survive in <1% of naive samples at 25%.
limits: Needs a known signal/distractor split per sample, which an agent lacks at run time. Gains are largest for smaller models.
agent_relevance: Fewer distractors help only if the relevant entry is kept. Supports relevance-aware pruning and warns against blind truncation.

source: Jonides & Nee (2006) Brain mechanisms of proactive interference in working memory (Neuroscience 139:181-193)
finding: In the recent-probes task, a probe that was in the previous trial's set but not the current one (recent negative) is rejected more slowly and less accurately. Left inferior frontal gyrus (BA45) is the main site that resolves it, seen in imaging, lesion and TMS work.
numbers: Monsell (1978): recent negatives cost about 75 ms and 7% accuracy. Patient M.L. (left frontal lesion): interference effect 5.9 SD above controls, almost 400 ms outside control range; accuracy effect 25%, 12% outside control range. Older adults show a larger effect and less IFG activity. Letters vs objects: RT effects 34 and 38 ms.
limits: Mostly one paradigm, very small patient numbers, verbal-heavy. The region may serve other selection demands.
agent_relevance: Resolving PI looks like a separate control step, not free. A scaffold step 'check the competitors for this cue' is the analogue.

source: Jonides & Nee (2006) Brain mechanisms of proactive interference in working memory (Neuroscience 139:181-193)
finding: Individual differences: higher working-memory span goes with better resolution of proactive interference. Postle & Brush (2004) pooled 7 studies to look at PI build-up across trial position. Directed-forgetting probes still cost time.
numbers: Directed-forgetting probes ('to be forgotten') were worse than controls by 136 ms and 2.6% accuracy (Zhang et al., 2003), with higher left-IFG activation.
limits: Review; effect sizes are quoted from original studies and not recomputed. Span link is correlational.
agent_relevance: Telling a person (or a model) to forget an item still leaves a cost on that item, as in b03.

source: Mercer (2025) Familiarity influences on proactive interference in verbal memory (QJEP 78(9):2008-2021)
finding: Recent-probes task with 8 targets per trial (N=192 online UK adults). PI appears (more errors for probes from the previous trial) but its size depends on stimulus familiarity: strongest for repeated non-words, weakest for unique non-words. Time since the previous trial did not matter.
numbers: PI (RN minus NRN error): repeating non-words 0.19, repeating words 0.12, unique words 0.13, unique non-words 0.06. Unique vs repeating non-words d=1.12, BF10=33,328; repeating non-words vs repeating words d=-0.62, BF10=12.9; repeating vs unique words d=0.13, BF10=0.26 (null). Condition Ns: 54, 47, 42, 49.
limits: Online sample, eight-item sets. Words vs non-words confounds meaning with prior long-term memory.
agent_relevance: Repeated, easily confused items create the most interference. Lessons built from repeated boilerplate may interfere more than distinct ones.

source: Mercer (2025) Familiarity influences on proactive interference in verbal memory (QJEP 78(9):2008-2021), reviewing Gardiner et al. (1972), Tehan & Humphreys (1996), Ozekin & McElree (2007)
finding: Release from PI depends on retrieval cues, not on change of material alone. Gardiner et al.: switching subcategory (wildflowers to garden flowers) released PI only when participants were told the subcategory to retrieve. Tehan & Humphreys: PI occurs only if the recall cue also fits the interfering item.
numbers: Ozekin & McElree (2007): 8 participants tested extensively; category switched every three trials (fruit to animals); PI affected familiarity at retrieval. No numbers for Gardiner or Tehan in this text.
limits: Secondhand through a recent paper; original numbers not opened.
agent_relevance: Category change helps only if the lookup cue selects the new category. A category tag on each lesson matters only if retrieval uses it.

source: Hubbard, Weaver, Turner & Rypma (2018) Re-examination of 'release-from-PI' phenomena: recall accuracy does not recover after a semantic switch. Memory 26(9):1191-1205
finding: Two experiments with inducement, semantic-switch and return epochs found no release from PI after a category switch. Recall kept falling across epochs. The authors propose 'reintroduction of PI' instead.
numbers: Numbers not obtained; abstract-level summary from a search result only.
limits: Null result against the classic release effect. A later ERP study (Huang et al., 2020) reported recall rising on the last trial after a shift, so the literature is split. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Do not assume rotating category fully resets interference. Test it in our own ablation.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Interference theory (secondary review)
finding: Reports classic numbers: Greenberg & Underwood (1950) paired adjectives, recall after 2 days about 70% for list 1, about 40% for list 2, about 25% for list 3. PI is less common than RI but larger for conceptually related items. A 'not to remember' cue reduced PI where 'not to recall' did not (Turvey & Wittlinger).
numbers: Competition vs unlearning is still debated (Barnes & Underwood 1959: A-C responses outnumber A-B after delay, read as unlearning). Briggs (1954): B items recovered spontaneously after 24 hours. Wohldmann et al. (2008): mental practice gives less RI than physical practice.
limits: Page is flagged as unclear and too technical; numbers are secondhand and the wording is ambiguous.
agent_relevance: Related items cause the biggest loss; unrelated ones do little. Same direction as b13.

source: Wickens, Born & Allen (1963); Wickens (1970) release from proactive inhibition
finding: Repeated same-category trials in the Brown-Peterson task lower recall trial by trial; a trial from a new category brings recall back toward first-trial level. Size of release varies with how different the new category is.
numbers: Exact numbers not opened this session.
limits: Later work finds release depends on retrieval cues (b20) and is not always found (b21). Not opened.
agent_relevance: Basis for the 'vary category' rule; treat as medium confidence until our own ablation.

source: Keppel & Underwood (1962) Proactive inhibition in short-term retention of single items. JVLVB 1:153-161
finding: Re-analysis of the Brown-Peterson design: on the first trial little is forgotten over seconds; forgetting grows with the number of earlier trials. Much of 'short-term decay' is proactive interference.
numbers: Exact percentages not opened this session (summary only from a search result).
limits: Later work argues some loss is not interference-based; not opened.
agent_relevance: Old items hurt more as they accumulate: a reason to bound library size per class.

source: Underwood (1957) Interference and forgetting. Psychological Review 64:49-60
finding: Pooled earlier studies: 24-hour forgetting depends mostly on how many lists were learned before, not on time itself.
numbers: Not opened; textbook figures (first list high, many prior lists far lower) not verified here.
limits: Later studies show competition and unlearning both matter; pooled-study design has confounds.
agent_relevance: Original ground for the proactive build-up rule.

source: Feredoes, Tononi & Postle (2006) Direct evidence for a prefrontal contribution to the control of proactive interference in verbal working memory. PNAS
finding: Repetitive TMS over left inferior frontal gyrus selectively impaired control of high-conflict probes in the recent-probes task.
numbers: Numbers not opened (search summary only).
limits: Causal evidence for a control step; TMS samples are small. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports a conflict-resolution step that is separate from storage.

source: Anderson & Neely (1996) Interference and inhibition in memory retrieval (handbook chapter)
finding: Review of competition-based and inhibition-based accounts of retrieval interference; later work cites it as the base for retrieval-induced forgetting ideas.
numbers: Not opened; full text not found.
limits: Inhibition accounts remain disputed.
agent_relevance: Rival theory to pure competition: strengthening one memory may suppress rivals.

source: Mercer (2025) Familiarity influences on proactive interference in verbal memory (QJEP 78(9):2008-2021) (intro: Samrani & Persson 2024; Samrani et al. 2017; Hamilton & Martin 2007; Engle 2002)
finding: Moderators of PI named in the intro: older age worsens PI control; short-term memory deficits exaggerate it; managing PI may be a main job of working memory.
numbers: Stated as established; no new numbers.
limits: Secondhand through one intro paragraph.
agent_relevance: Interference control varies by person; for models it varies by family (b08, b05).
